citation: An ecological perspective on children's play with digital technologies in South Africa and the United Kingdom (Journal of Psychology in Africa)

claims.text: Digital engagement is validated by educational utility because technology is valued primarily as a route out of poverty rather than for entertainment
objections: Does this help with education or is it just for entertainment?

claims.text: Shared device scarcity creates parent-child congruence because limited hardware creates overlapping digital practices that put parents in a stronger position to support their child's use, though this does not guarantee active co-play
objections: Can we use this together on our shared device?

claims.text: Inconsistent connectivity mandates offline functionality because intermittent access renders always-online products impractical despite perceived need
objections: Will it work when the internet is not consistent?

claims.text: Home-school projects bridge resource gaps because classroom device scarcity necessitates extending digital ecologies into domestic spaces
Intergenerational mediation enables adoption because skilled elders provide the family-supported knowledge transfer necessary to navigate technology
objections: Can my grandmother help me understand how to use this?

confidence: Qualitative survey and case study data from South Africa and UK; mechanisms derived from author interpretation of parental and teacher perspectives, magnitudes unknown
